P: How designers are evolving their tools, craft, and teams with AI
P: BY DESIGNER FUND IN PARTNERSHIP WITH FOUNDATION CAPITAL
H1: In 2025, designers were experimenting with AI. In 2026, they’re rebuilding around it.
H4: Interviews with practitioners and leaders
P: AI in Design 2026 aims to capture how AI is transforming tech design across designers’ desks and within their teams.

P: We ran our first AI in Design survey in early 2025 because we consistently heard designers and leaders ask, “How are others doing this, and what’s working?” A year later, we’re attempting to get a sense for what’s changed and share firsthand perspectives.

P: The answers come from over 900 designers at startups, enterprises, and agencies who work across disciplines like product design, brand design, research, and design engineering. We also conducted over 20 interviews with leaders at companies actively navigating this shift.
A: Sign up for new releases.
H4: AI is sparking a creative renaissance in design. With new instruments, it’s our chance to compose wholly new music.

P: AI usage has surged, but the toolstack is still in flux. Designers are using double the number of off-the-shelf tools than they did in 2025, and they’re building custom software with AI that matches how they like to work. As everyone rushes to keep up with new releases, reliable output quality remains the largest area for improvement.

H1: Craft in the age of infinite output

P: Everyone is shipping faster. But is speed good for craft? AI has unlocked a new gear for designers: they’re ideating faster, prototyping more, and learning to code. Half of respondents have pushed AI-generated code to production. At the same time, we hear concerns about craft atrophy and the loneliness of designing alongside AI instead of teammates.

P: The trend toward designers as builders

P: AI gave designers new powers. Now organizations need to adapt. Roles are blurring as designers take on PM and engineering work, and vice versa. Hiring managers want AI fluency alongside a high bar for craft, vision, and storytelling. But few companies have updated performance reviews, team structures, or hiring practices to match how the work has changed.
